title: YouTube as a source of (mis)information for morning sickness self-help - A content analysis and literature review of recommendations for nausea and vomiting in pregnancy
screen_reason: Content analysis of the 45 most-watched English YouTube videos on nausea and vomiting in pregnancy, from which 85 unique recommendations were extracted and then each classified against a systematic literature review as Effective / Ineffective / Potentially Unsafe / Unclear / Not Investigated. That yields a share of claims judged against external evidence: 4/85 (4.7%) potentially unsafe (a CONTENT-type falsity/harm judgement) and 8/85 (9.4%) evidence-based (a QUALITY-type evidence-concordance share). Important caveat carried on both rows: the denominator is 85 unique RECOMMENDATION TYPES, not videos or content items, so it is not weighted by how often each recommendation appears.

estimates.country: Videos uploaded mainly from the USA (n=28, 62.2%) and India (n=7, 15.6%), with Canada, Netherlands, UK, UAE and unknown
estimates.date: Videos collected December 2022 - October 2023 (videos themselves uploaded 2008-2022, most 2018-2020); literature review completed December 2023
estimates.measure_type: % of unique morning-sickness (NVP) recommendations made in YouTube videos that a literature review judged potentially unsafe
estimates.value_raw: n = 4, 4.7 % (peppermint, chamomile, fennel, CBD oil/cannabinoids); Abstract: "5% were potentially unsafe"
estimates.denominator: 85 unique NVP recommendations identified by inductive content analysis of the 45 most-watched full-length English-language YouTube videos offering NVP advice
estimates.definition: A recommendation counted in the numerator if the authors' literature review classified it 'Potentially Unsafe: Linked to adverse effects that may endanger pregnancy' -- here peppermint, chamomile and fennel (contraindicated, possible miscarriage and adverse neonatal effects) and CBD oil/other cannabinoids (FDA advises against; cross the placental barrier)
estimates.misinfo_def: "Health misinformation refers to any false or misleading information about health that is not backed by evidence."
estimates.source_quote: Several recommendations in the videos were deemed potentially unsafe ( n = 4, 4.7 %).
estimates.page_loc: Results, 'Potentially unsafe recommendations', pp. 4-5; the four are named in the next sentences (peppermint, chamomile and fennel 'are contraindicated in pregnancy because they may cause miscarriages and other adverse neonatal effects'; 'CBD oil and other cannabinoids are deemed potentially unsafe'); Abstract: '5% were potentially unsafe'
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Authors' own systematic literature review per recommendation: two keyword searches each (title-field then any-field) through the KU Leuven LIMO multi-database system (PubMed, Web of Science, JSTOR, Springer), peer-reviewed articles only, judged on Evans' hierarchy-of-evidence framework (systematic reviews/meta-analyses > RCTs > observational; qualitative excluded). Phase-1 coding by three authors with a coding log, discrepancies resolved by consensus; evidence judgements discussed to consensus within the team. NO inter-rater reliability statistic is reported for either phase, and the authors note they did not conduct a full GRADE assessment.
estimates.moderator_quote: Videos were identified through targeted keyword searches combining symptom-related terms ('nausea', 'vomiting', 'morning sickness') with pregnancy-related terms ('first trimester', 'pregnancy') and advice-related terms ('tips and tricks', 'do's and don'ts', 'recommendations')... Search results were sorted by total number of 'views' to prioritize content with greater potential inﬂuence and public health relevance.
estimates.notes: borderline=true for two reasons an adjudicator should weigh. (1) The label is a SAFETY judgement ('linked to adverse effects that may endanger pregnancy') rather than a strict truth/falsity judgement; I coded CONTENT because recommending a substance contraindicated in pregnancy is a claim contradicted by external evidence, i.e. misleading health content, and the paper itself is framed as a study of '(mis)information'. (2) THE DENOMINATOR IS UNUSUAL: 85 unique recommendation TYPES, deduplicated across 45 videos, so a recommendation appearing in 30 videos (ginger) weighs exactly the same as one appearing in a single video. This is a share of the ADVICE REPERTOIRE, not a share of content items or of what audiences saw, and it is therefore not directly comparable with item-level prevalence estimates. denom_selection=curated because the video set is a view-ranked top-N built to theoretical saturation.

estimates.country: Videos uploaded mainly from the USA (n=28, 62.2%) and India (n=7, 15.6%), with Canada, Netherlands, UK, UAE and unknown
estimates.date: Videos collected December 2022 - October 2023 (videos uploaded 2008-2022); literature review completed December 2023
estimates.measure_type: % of unique morning-sickness (NVP) recommendations made in YouTube videos that were confirmed effective by the evidence (i.e. evidence-based)
estimates.value_raw: only eight (9.4 %) of 85 were confirmed to be effective; Abstract: "fewer than 10% were evidence-based"
estimates.denominator: 85 unique NVP recommendations identified by inductive content analysis of the 45 most-watched full-length English-language YouTube videos offering NVP advice
estimates.definition: A recommendation counted in the numerator if the literature review classified it 'Effective: Supported by multiple studies showing symptom reduction' (vitamin B6, ginger, and six specific pharmacological interventions)
estimates.misinfo_def: "Health misinformation refers to any false or misleading information about health that is not backed by evidence."
estimates.source_quote: Of the 85 recommendations provided in the videos, only eight (9.4 %) were confirmed to be effective based on available evidence
estimates.page_loc: Results, 'Effective recommendations', p. 4; also Abstract (Results) and Discussion
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Same evidence-verification procedure as the row above: per-recommendation literature review on Evans' hierarchy of evidence, consensus judgements among three authors, no IRR statistic, no GRADE.
estimates.moderator_quote: Recommendations identiﬁed in phase one were then categorized based on a literature review into: Effective: Supported by multiple studies showing symptom reduction; Ineffective: Evidence showing no effect or worsening symptoms; Potentially Unsafe: Linked to adverse effects that may endanger pregnancy; Unclear Effectiveness: Limited or contradictory evidence; Not Investigated: No studies or published ﬁndings
estimates.notes: Coded QUALITY, not CONTENT, and flagged for exclusion from prevalence: 'evidence-based' is a positive evidence-concordance bar, and its complement (90.6% not confirmed effective) is dominated by ABSENCE of evidence -- 48.2% unclear/limited evidence and 36.5% never studied -- not by demonstrated falsity. Recording it because it is the paper's headline claim ('fewer than 10% were evidence-based'), so an adjudicator sees the number and its correct interpretation. I did NOT compute the 90.6% complement (R8 forbids computed complements). Same recommendation-type denominator caveat as the row above.

missed_or_uncertain: Not extracted, with reasons: (1) 'Ineffective' recommendations: 'Seeking social support was the only recommendation that was found to be ineffective', i.e. n=1, giving 1/85 = 1.2%. This is the only category that is squarely a demonstrated-falsity judgement, but it is a single item, no percentage is printed, and a one-item estimate fails R4 (quality over quantity). Recorded here so an adjudicator can add it if the review wants the strictest falsity category. (2) 'Unclear Effectiveness' n = 41, 48.2% and 'Not Investigated' n = 31, 36.5%. Both are absence-of-evidence categories, not falsity, so neither is a misinformation prevalence; note that 8+1+4+41+31 = 85 exactly, so the five categories are exhaustive and mutually exclusive. (3) The combined 'ineffective or potentially unsafe' figure (5/85 = 5.9%) would be a cross-category sum I computed -- forbidden by R8. (4) Recommendation FREQUENCIES across videos (ginger mentioned in 66.7% of videos, frequent small meals 62.2%, talk to an HCP 60%) are shares of videos mentioning a given piece of advice, not shares of content that is false, so they are not prevalence estimates. (5) Figures quoted from other studies in the Introduction (D'Souza et al., 'over 20% of YouTube's most viewed videos on epidural labor analgesia contain non-factual information'; van Gelder et al., 'over 40% of social media posts on medication use during pregnancy contradict current risk knowledge') are cited from elsewhere -- excluded by R8. (6) The paper reports NO video-level misinformation share (e.g. % of the 45 videos containing at least one unsafe recommendation), which is the figure a prevalence review would most want; it is simply not computed.

rob.design: Two-phase study. Phase 1: inductive qualitative content analysis (Elo & Kyngas) of English-language full-length YouTube videos offering NVP advice, collected December 2022 - October 2023 via targeted keyword searches (symptom x pregnancy x advice terms derived from a scoping search), results sorted by view count. Exclusions: HCP-targeted advice, hyperemesis-only, vlogs without recommendations, non-English, non-pregnancy nausea, other complications, illegible audio, YouTube shorts. Initial 30 videos (master's thesis dataset) expanded in rounds of five until theoretical saturation (no new conceptual codes in five consecutive videos); saturation reached at video 39, final n=45. Transcripts downloaded and corrected against the videos; unit of analysis the transcript, coding focused on discrete recommendations; both direct and indirect recommendations counted; coding by three authors with a coding log, discrepancies resolved by consensus. NO kappa or other IRR statistic reported. Phase 2: per-recommendation literature review (two keyword searches each) via KU Leuven's LIMO multi-database system, peer-reviewed only, judged on Evans' hierarchy of evidence, qualitative studies excluded; recommendations classified Effective / Ineffective / Potentially Unsafe / Unclear Effectiveness / Not Investigated; first pass by two authors on the initial 30 videos, full review completed by the first author, judgements discussed to team consensus. Authors note no full GRADE assessment was done. Sample skews US (62.2%) and Indian (15.6%); mean video 7'44" and 222,742 views; three creators contributed multiple videos.
